summary: This experimental document extends the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) to work on connections that pass through NATs and NAPTs. It changes the data used to compute traffic keys but does not alter TCP-AO's packet processing or key generation algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret handshake breaks when a middleman rewrites the addresses. This fixes the handshake to still work.

questions: using tcp authentication option through nat
how does tcp-ao work through nat
subtitle: Extending TCP Authentication to work through network address translators

tldr.problem: TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) authenticates TCP connections by including IP addresses and ports in its message authentication codes, but NATs translate these addresses, breaking authentication.
tldr.mechanism: TCP-AO-NAT adds flags to zero out the translated addresses and ports during authentication key generation, allowing the protocol to work transparently through NATs.
tldr.outcome: TCP-AO can now protect connections passing through NATs without modification to packet processing or key generation algorithms.

facts.label: Use case
facts.value: Client/server with clients behind NAT, multipath TCP

today: RFC 6978 is an Experimental protocol that extends TCP-AO to work with NATs by zeroing out translated addresses during authentication. It has not been obsoleted and remains a mechanism for deploying authenticated TCP connections in networks with address translation.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
TCP-AO (TCP Authentication Option) is a protocol that authenticates TCP connections, making sure the data comes from who it claims to be. It works by including information from the TCP connection in a calculation that produces a unique code called a Message Authentication Code (MAC).

This information includes the local and remote IP addresses, the TCP ports, and the initial sequence numbers. However, when a connection passes through a NAT (Network Address Translator) or NAPT (Network Address and Port Translator), these devices rewrite the source address and port numbers. TCP-AO would then reject the connection as inauthentic because the addresses no longer match.

TCP-AO-NAT solves this by allowing the protocol to ignore the addresses and ports during authentication, treating them as if they were zero. Both endpoints must agree to use this mode for the same connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret code is calculated using your address. When a middleman changes your address, the code breaks. TCP-AO-NAT makes the code calculation not care about the address, so it works anyway.

sections.title: How TCP-AO Works Today
sections.content:
TCP-AO generates unique traffic keys for each socket pair. These keys are created using six pieces of information from the connection:

  • IP local address
  • IP remote address
  • TCP local port
  • TCP remote port
  • TCP local Initial Sequence Number (ISN)
  • TCP remote Initial Sequence Number (ISN)

All of these are used in the MAC calculation for normal segments. For SYN segments during connection setup, the remote ISN is unknown, so it is omitted.

When a NAT rewrites the source address or port, the receiving end computes a different key and rejects the segment as tampered with. This is correct security behavior in normal conditions, but it prevents the connection from working at all when NATs are present.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret code uses six pieces of information about your connection. When a middleman changes two of those pieces (your address and port), the receiving side calculates a different code and thinks you are lying.

sections.title: The TCP-AO-NAT Extension
sections.content:
TCP-AO-NAT adds two new flags to the Master Key Tuple (MKT), the data structure that holds TCP-AO parameters for a connection:

  • localNAT: when set, the local IP address and port are zeroed before MAC calculation
  • remoteNAT: when set, the remote IP address and port are zeroed before MAC calculation

These flags modify how traffic keys are computed and how MAC values are calculated. Instead of using the actual addresses and ports, the algorithm treats them as zero values. This requires no changes to the key derivation algorithm itself, only to the data fed into it.

Both endpoints must agree on the same flag settings. A client behind a NAT would set localNAT=TRUE for outgoing connections. A server accepting connections from behind NATs would set remoteNAT=TRUE. Peer-to-peer applications might set both flags to support connections through symmetric NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: When zeroing the address, both sides must agree beforehand. A client says, 'Ignore my address,' and the server agrees. Then they both pretend the address is zero when calculating the code.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Zeroing the addresses and ports reduces the randomness of the input to the key derivation function. With IPv4, this changes the input from two IP addresses, two ISNs, and two ports down to just two ISNs when both flags are set.

However, this trade-off is considered acceptable because the IP addresses and dynamically assigned ports typically have less randomness than the ISNs (Initial Sequence Numbers). The randomness of the ISNs dominates the calculation, so removing the addresses and ports has minimal security impact.

Connections that do not use the NAT flags are completely unaffected. TCP-AO-NAT is not intended for Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) that translate in-band data like FTP or SIP, because TCP-AO-NAT would correctly interpret such alterations as attacks on the TCP segments themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Removing the address from the code makes the code less random, but not much. The code gets its randomness mostly from the sequence numbers, which are still there. So it is still pretty secure.
